ASK:
What are some differences in aircraft handling during the initial rotation and liftoff? (FCTM 3.31)
Answer: During a normal all engine takeoff, a smooth continuous rotation toward a target pitch is initiated at VR. With an engine inoperative, a smooth continuous rotation is also initiated at VR; however, the target pitch attitude is approximately 2° to 3° below the normal all engine pitch attitude. The rate of rotation with an engine inoperative is also slightly slower (1/2° per second less) than that for a normal takeoff. After liftoff adjust pitch attitude to maintain the desired speed. If the engine failure occurs at or after liftoff, apply rudder and aileron to control heading and keep the wings level. In flight, correct rudder input will center the control wheel. To center the control wheel, rudder is required in the direction that the control wheel is displaced. This approximates a minimum drag configuration.

What will be indicated on the engine instruments in the event of an engine failure at takeoff? (Standards Q&A > Engine Inop Takeoff – 747, FCOM Vol.1 MAN 1.6, pg.4)
Answer: Loss/ no indication on N1, red boxed EGT, (Primary) no N2 (if exceedance detected), oil pressure (if exceedance detected)(secondary)

Should you increase thrust on the operating engines (fixed derate) in the event of an engine failure? (FCOM: MAN.1.9)
Answer: During a fixed derate takeoff, a thrust increase following an engine failure could result in loss of directional control and should not be accomplished unless, in the opinion of the captain, terrain contact is imminent. This is because the takeoff speeds consider VMCG and VMCA only at the fixed derate level of thrust.

After verifying CON thrust, what is the purpose of selecting and executing the ENG OUT prompt? (FCOM: Vol. 2 11.31.39)
Answer: “Condition: Selecting the ENG OUT> prompt on the VNAV CLB page displays applicable engine out performance data. Execution activates engine out performance data and terminates the VNAV engine out takeoff phase. Result: the FMC engine out climb function is active, the pitch mode is VNAV SPD, the command speed is E/O SPD, and the reference thrust limit is CON. The use of VNAV for descent and approach is enabled.”

ASK:
Are there any procedural differences we should incorporate into our approach briefing? (FCOM Vol. 1 MAN.2.2)
Answer: Approach and landing have no differences in procedure as per the Profile in FCOM Vol. 1 MAN.2.2

Why should you minimize thrust lever movements during final approach? (FCTM 5.30)
Answer: Full rudder authority and rudder pedal steering capability are not affected by rudder trim. If touchdown occurs with the rudder still trimmed for the approach, be prepared for the higher rudder pedal forces required to track the centerline on rollout.

How soon should the transition to manual flight be planned? (FCTM 6.8-9)
Answer: When a manual landing is planned from an approach with the autopilot engaged, the transition to manual flight should be planned early enough to allow the pilot time to establish airplane control before beginning the flare. The PF should consider disengaging the autopilot and disconnecting the autothrottle 1 to 2 nm before the threshold, or approximately 300 to 600 feet above field elevation.

For a multi-autopilot go-around, how is yaw initially controlled? (FCTM 5.69)
Answer: For a multi-autopilot go-around, yaw is initially controlled by the autopilot. Be prepared to immediately apply rudder input when selecting another roll mode, pitch mode, or when altitude capture occurs above 400 feet AGL because the autopilot reverts to single autopilot operation. Automatic control of rudder is discontinued.

When performing a go-around in the 747-8, how does the automation sequence differ from the 747-400, and how may those differences affect your plan during an engine inoperative go-around?(FCTM 5.81)
Answer: In a multi-autopilot go-around, yaw is initially controlled by the autopilot. Be prepared to immediately apply rudder input when selecting another roll or pitch mode, or upon automatic transition from TO/GA to LNAV. At that point the autopilot reverts to single autopilot operation and automatic rudder control is discontinued.

ASK:
With engine 1 inoperative, what is the correct way of using the thrust reversers on landing if greater than reverse idle is necessary? (FCTM 6.33-34, FCOM Vol. 1 55.1)
Answer: Symmetrical reverse thrust should be used with one or two engines inoperative, if possible. Use normal reverse thrust procedures and techniques. All thrust levers may be brought to the reverse idle position; then apply reverse thrust on symmetrical engines as needed.

Is this also appropriate when a T/R has been deferred? (FCTM 6.33-34, FCOM Vol. 1 55.1 )
Answer: OPERATIONS (O)
The REV amber indication and ENG _ REVERSER message may be displayed for the deactivated reverser.
Use symmetrical reverse as required.

Why is it so important to establish the desired reverse thrust level as soon as possible after touchdown? (FCTM 6.26)
Answer: Reverse thrust is most effective at high speeds. After touchdown, with the thrust levers at idle, rapidly raise the reverse thrust levers up and aft to the interlock position, then apply reverse thrust as required.

At what speed should the thrust reversers be at reverse idle during the deceleration? (FCOM Vol. 1 NP.55.1)
Answer: If stopping is assured, by 80 knots, start movement of the reverse thrust levers to be at the reverse idle detent by 60 knots. After the engines are at reverse idle, move the reverse thrust levers full down.

SAY: In cruise flight at 35,000’ and 105 miles from the nearest airport we experience a FIRE MAIN DECK warning. Weather is CAVOK with calm winds on the ground and the landing distance for the usable runway is 11,500’. 

ASK:
What guidance do we have to verify that this is not a FALSE CARGO FIRE WARNING?  (FCOM Vol. 1 SP.2.6)
Answer: Synoptic displays are provided as a means of assisting the flight crew in rapidly understanding the status of the airplane systems. However, crews should not rely solely on the displays for determining airplane status. Synoptic displays should only be used as necessary to get the desired information and then deselected. The clarity and simplicity of displayed information enable the flight crew to obtain necessary information from a brief scan. If the flight crew elects to use synoptic displays in conjunction with accomplishment of procedures, they must assure no distraction from the intended task results. This is particularly true when accomplishing non-normal procedures. Under certain conditions, system faults can result in missing synoptic information. Therefore, decisions regarding non-normal situations should be based on EICAS messages and other flight deck effects and indications. In every case where a non-normal procedure results in a need for memory items, they should be completed before selecting a synoptic display. Accomplishment of necessary procedures should take priority over use of synoptic displays. There have been several false fir

ASK:
Which EICAS alert category requires immediate crew awareness and corrective action to maintain safe flight? (FCTM 1.1)
Answer: Alerts are categorized into four categories which are prioritized by the urgency of the required pilot response. Each of these use alert colors that are consistent with industry standards and requirements:
Time critical warnings (red)
Warnings (red)
Cautions (amber)
Advisories (amber)
The function of the Master Warning and Master Caution lights are to provide crew awareness to alerts. After completing an NNC, the flight crew should review all EICAS alert messages to determine the need to do other NNCs.

What is the procedure if there are multiple malfunctions? (FCTM 8.2)
Answer: Display and Manipulation of EICAS MessagesIf more than one EICAS alert message is displayed, the messages are displayed in a list which is grouped by priority level. EICAS warning messages are displayed in red at the top of the message list. EICAS caution messages are displayed in amber below the lowest warning message. EICAS advisory messages are displayed in amber below the lowest caution message and are indented one character so they may be distinguished from EICAS caution messages. The most recent EICAS alert message is displayed at the top of its priority group and all messages move down one display line. If a message is no longer displayed because the respective system non-normal condition no longer exists, all messages previously displayed move up one display line

Answer: Level off at the lowest safe altitude or 14,000 feet (10,000 feet if applicable), whichever is higher. Lowest safe altitude is the Minimum Enroute Altitude (MEA), Minimum Off Route Altitude (MORA), or any other altitude based on terrain clearance, navigation aid reception, or other appropriate criteria.

SAY:
We have confirmed the presence of a main deck fire and have decided to execute an expedited freighter descent and immediate landing.

ASK:
What procedures should be followed during this event? (QRH 8.22 FIRE MAIN DECK; FCTM 8)
Answer: Oxygen masks and smoke goggles on, crew communications established. Accomplish the FIRE MAIN DECK non-normal checklist (QRH 8.22) in sequence: the PF flies and begins the expedited descent, the PM reads and does the checklist. The checklist arms the main deck fire system, configures the air systems and depressurizes the airplane to reduce the airflow feeding the fire (the reason FL250 is the target altitude), then directs landing at the nearest suitable airport. Do not delay the descent to troubleshoot; plan the approach for the nearest usable runway.

When should ATC be advised of your emergency descent? (FOM 11; FCTM 8)
Answer: As soon as the immediate actions are complete and the descent has started: declare MAYDAY, state the main deck fire, request direct routing to the nearest suitable airport and the lowest usable altitude, and advise souls on board and fuel remaining when able (the sim script expects these calls). The PM handles communications while the PF flies the descent, and keeps ATC updated as the plan develops.

What are some ways to ensure terrain awareness? (FCTM 8; approach chart minimum altitudes)
Answer: Check the MSA/MORA and the approach chart minimum altitudes before the descent, select terrain on the ND, respect any E

ASK:
As a crew, how will you manage a low-speed engine failure while the FO is setting thrust and the Captain’s hand is not yet on the thrust levers? Who calls it out, who decides, and how is control transferred? (FCOM: MAN)
Possible Answers:
Brief the RTO in the Takeoff Briefing (FOM 11.1.29).
Whoever observes the failure calls it out immediately (FCOM MAN.1.2).
The FO maintains control, reducing thrust as needed, until the Captain makes a positive input to the controls. The Captain announces “REJECT” and assumes control.
The Captain alone decides to reject.
